oracle: To avoid the risk of being left with a part they consider smaller.
answer: Because the second person picks first, the second person will always take the piece they consider larger, leaving the first person with the other piece. So the first person cannot benefit from cutting unevenly: any advantage built into one piece becomes a certain loss in the piece that remains. Cutting the cake into two pieces the first person considers equal is the only way for the first person to guarantee a fair, at-least-half share no matter which piece the second person takes.

oracle: We check “microbes on hands” (or equivalently “covering of the food reduces cases”), because the result separates the two hypotheses.
answer: The minimum information needed is a single observation that behaves differently under H1 (transmission is through hands) and under H2 (transmission is direct through food): Test the food itself for the microbe before anyone touches it with unwashed hands: if the food is already contaminated at that point, H2 is supported; if the food is clean until after hand contact, H1 is supported. A shared observation, such as "the person became ill", does not help because both hypotheses predict it equally, so seeing it leaves the two hypotheses exactly as likely as before. A discriminating observation helps because it is predicted by one hypothesis and not the other, so its outcome rules one of them out.

A shared observation, such as "no sound was detected", does not help because both hypotheses predict it equally, so seeing it leaves the two hypotheses exactly as likely as before. A discriminating observation helps because it is predicted by one hypothesis and not the other, so its outcome rules one of them out.
